title: Review: Moments, levers and gears (physics only); Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Physics (8463) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.5.5-c16, 4.5.5-c04, 4.5.4-c02, 4.5.4-c03. Clues: 4.5.5-c16 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.5.5-c04 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.5.4-c02 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.5.4-c03 written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: 4.5.4-q13, 4.5.4-q14, 4.5.4-q15, 4.5.4-q16, 4.5.4-q09, 4.5.5-q10, 4.5.5-q24, 4.5.4-q05, 4.5.5-q08, 4.5.5-q23, 4.5.4-q12, 4.5.5-q01, 4.5.5-q17, 4.5.5-q18, 4.5.5-q19, 4.5.5-q20, 4.5.5-q21, 4.5.5-q22. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Pascal
items.clue: One newton acting on each square metre.

items.label: Pivot
items.clue: The fixed point about which an object turns.

items.label: Moment of a force
items.clue: The turning effect of a push or pull about a fixed point.

questions.stem: A beam is balanced on a pivot. A 100 N weight hangs 0.75 m to the left of the pivot, and a single weight hangs 1.5 m to the right. What is that weight?
questions.explanation: Anticlockwise moment = 100 x 0.75 = 75 Nm, so the unknown weight is 75 / 1.5 = 50 N.

questions.stem: A rod is balanced on a pivot. A 6.0 N force acts 0.50 m from the pivot on one side, and an 8.0 N force acts on the other side. How far from the pivot is the 8.0 N force?
questions.explanation: Clockwise moment = 6.0 x 0.50 = 3.0 Nm, so d = M / F = 3.0 / 8.0 = 0.375 m.

questions.stem: What do a simple lever and a simple gear system have in common?

options.text: Both give out more energy than is put into them by the user
Both can be used to transmit the rotational effects of forces
Both increase the size of the force that you apply to them
Both change a force's direction without turning anything

questions.explanation: This is what the specification says about them: each transmits the turning effect from one place to another.

questions.stem: Two gear wheels are meshed together and the smaller one is driven clockwise. How does the larger gear turn?

options.text: Clockwise too, because the teeth push it the same way round
Anticlockwise but faster, because it is the bigger wheel
Anticlockwise, more slowly, and with a larger moment
Anticlockwise but at the same rate, because the two are joined

questions.explanation: Meshed teeth reverse the sense; the larger wheel makes fewer turns per second and exerts a larger moment.

questions.stem: A force of 25 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 15 cm from a pivot. What is the moment of the force about the pivot?

options.text: 375 Nm

questions.explanation: 15 cm = 0.15 m, so M = F d = 25 x 0.15 = 3.75 Nm, with the distance in metres as the specification requires.

questions.stem: A walker on soft snow puts on wide snowshoes and stops sinking in. Why?

options.text: The larger area increases the pressure on the snow.
The larger area reduces the pressure on the snow.
The larger area presses down harder on the snow.
The force is the walker's mass, and wide shoes shrink it.

questions.explanation: The normal force is unchanged but is spread over more area, so p = F/A falls.

questions.stem: Explain why atmospheric pressure at the top of a mountain is lower than at sea level.

options.text: Gravity is much weaker at the top of a high mountain.
The air up there is colder, so it presses down less hard.
There is less air above, so fewer molecules collide.
The wind is stronger high up, blowing the air away.

questions.explanation: Fewer air molecules above the surface means less weight of air and fewer collisions with it.

questions.stem: Which row gives the units to use in the equation M = F d?

options.text: M in newton-metres, F in grams, d in metres
M in newton-metres, F in newtons, d in metres
M in newtons, F in newtons, d in metres
M in joules, F in newtons, d in metres

questions.explanation: These are the units the specification gives: Nm for the moment, N for the force and m for the distance.

questions.stem: A force of 16 N acts normal to a surface of area 200 cm². Calculate the pressure in pascals. 1 m² = 10 000 cm²

options.text: 8 Pa
80 Pa
800 Pa

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a simple model of the Earth's atmosphere?

options.text: A deep layer of gas that gets denser as altitude rises.
A thick layer of air of the same density at all heights.
A layer of air about as deep as the Earth is wide.
A thin layer of air round the Earth that thins with altitude.

questions.explanation: The specification describes a thin layer, relative to the size of the Earth, that gets less dense with altitude.

questions.stem: A plank balances on a pivot. A 10 N weight sits 0.60 m to the left of the pivot, and a 30 N weight sits somewhere to the right. What can be said about the 30 N weight?

options.text: It sits further from the pivot, because a larger force turns more
It sits closer to the pivot, because its force is the larger
It sits the same distance out, as the plank is balanced
It cannot balance, since the two forces are not equal

questions.explanation: Equal moments with a larger force means a smaller distance: 0.20 m, one third of 0.60 m.

questions.stem: In physics, what is meant by the term 'fluid'?

options.text: A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.
A liquid only, since a gas cannot be poured.
Anything that pours, such as dry sand.
A gas only, as gases fill any space.

questions.explanation: The specification states that a fluid can be either a liquid or a gas; both can flow and both exert pressure.

questions.stem: Two tanks are filled to the same depth, one with water and one with mercury. Why is the pressure at the base greater in the mercury?

options.text: Mercury is denser, so the column above weighs more.
The mercury must be filled to a greater depth.
Mercury is denser, so its column is taller than water.
Mercury fills up more volume at the same depth here.

questions.explanation: In p = h ρ g the height is the same, so the greater density gives the greater pressure.

questions.stem: Calculate the pressure due to a column of water of height 25 m. density of water = 1000 kg/m³  gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg

options.text: 245 Pa

questions.stem: A diver swims from a depth of 8.0 m to a depth of 12.0 m. density of sea water = 1030 kg/m³  gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg  Calculate the increase in pressure on the diver.

options.text: 420 Pa

questions.stem: A sealed can is held completely under water. Why does the water exert a resultant upward force on it?

options.text: Water pushes up on the bottom and not down on the top.
The can is full of air, which is lighter than the water.
Only the bottom face has water pushing on it.
Pressure on its bottom face exceeds that on its top.

questions.explanation: The bottom face is deeper, so the pressure there is greater and the resultant force is upwards.

questions.stem: A submerged object experiences a greater pressure on its bottom surface than on its top surface. What is the resultant upward force called?

options.text: The force by which upthrust beats weight.
The upthrust on the object.
A normal contact force from the water below.
The water's push under its base only.

questions.explanation: The specification names this resultant upward force the upthrust.

questions.stem: A solid block is lowered into a tank of water and floats. Which statement explains why it floats?

options.text: Its density is lower than the density of the water.
It is lighter than water, whatever its size or shape.
The upthrust on it is larger than its own weight.
It has a large volume and holds a lot of air.

questions.explanation: Floating and sinking are decided by comparing the density of the object with that of the liquid.
